lead: Send symbols fast enough and each pulse is still ringing when the next one is sampled. The tail of every other symbol lands on this instant as intersymbol interference, or ISI, and it pushes the sample towards the wrong decision. Nyquist's criterion states exactly when the spill is zero: the overall pulse must cross zero at every other sampling instant. Every baseband modem, Ethernet PHY and DSL link is designed around this one condition.
prereq: You need: the Fourier transform and power spectral density (see Unit 1, Foundations), and the symbol period, PAM and line codes (see Unit 4, Sampling and Pulse Modulation).

sections.h3: The model: one pulse per symbol

blocks.text: A baseband link sends one symbol every T seconds. T is the symbol period, in seconds. The k-th symbol ak is one of M real levels: for binary, ±1; for 4-level PAM, ±1 and ±3. The symbol rate is Rs = 1/T baud, where one baud is one symbol per second. Each symbol carries log₂M bits, so the bit rate is Rb = Rs log₂M bit/s.

Three blocks shape the pulse. The transmit filter g<sub>T</sub>(t) turns each symbol into a waveform. The channel c(t) is the cable, fibre or radio path. The receive filter g<sub>R</sub>(t) limits noise before the sampler. Their cascade is one overall pulse p(t) = g<sub>T</sub>(t) * c(t) * g<sub>R</sub>(t), where * means convolution and p(t) is the shape a single symbol leaves at the sampler.
r(t) = Σ<sub>n</sub> a<sub>n</sub> p(t − nT) + n(t)
blocks.where: r(t) is the received signal before sampling; a<sub>n</sub> is the n-th symbol level; p(t) is the overall pulse; T is the symbol period in seconds; n(t) is additive noise.

blocks.text: y(kT) = a<sub>k</sub> p(0) + Σ<sub>n≠k</sub> a<sub>n</sub> p((k − n)T) + n(kT)
blocks.where: y(kT) is the sample taken at t = kT; a<sub>k</sub> p(0) is the wanted term, p(0) being the peak height; the middle sum is the intersymbol interference (ISI); n(kT) is the noise sample.

blocks.text: The middle sum is the damage: tails of all other symbols landing on this instant. Peak distortion D = (1/p(0)) Σn≠k |p(nT)| is the worst-case ISI as a fraction of the wanted amplitude. D = 0.25 means ISI can reach a quarter of the signal, shrinking the margin to the decision threshold by that much.

Kill every term of the ISI sum: require p(nT) = 0 for every integer n ≠ 0. This is Nyquist's first criterion, also called the zero-ISI condition. The overall pulse must pass through zero at every sampling instant except its own.

The pulse that meets it exactly is the sinc: p(t) = sinc(t/T) = sin(πt/T)/(πt/T), with p(0) = 1. The numerator vanishes whenever t/T is a nonzero integer, so all zeros fall on the neighbouring sampling instants. The figure shows two such pulses one period apart and their sum.
The criterion is a condition on p(t), the whole chain. A clean transmit filter with a distorting channel still gives ISI, which is why an equaliser at the receiver is often needed.

The sinc spectrum is a rectangle of width 1/(2T) = Rs/2 Hz on each side of zero. Zero ISI therefore needs at least W = Rs/2 Hz, the Nyquist bandwidth. For binary, Rs = Rb, so the ceiling is 2 bit/s/Hz; with M levels it becomes 2 log₂M bit/s/Hz.

Two catches. The sinc stretches from −∞ to +∞, so it is non-causal and cannot be built. Its tails decay only as 1/t, so truncating it, or sampling slightly off the ideal instant, breaks the zeros and ISI returns. The next chapter shows the raised cosine pulse that pays a little extra bandwidth for fast-decaying tails.

The Nyquist bandwidth is a floor, not a target. A binary link at 2400 bit/s cannot fit in less than 1200 Hz of baseband without ISI, because 2400 symbols per second each need to be resolved and the sinc that does it occupies R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 1200 Hz. Real designs spend 10% to 30% extra bandwidth on a raised cosine roll-off, so a practical 2400 bit/s link uses roughly 1320 Hz to 1560 Hz.

Raising M buys bit rate inside the same band. 4-level PAM at 2400 baud carries 4800 bit/s in the same 1200 Hz floor, that is 4 bit/s/Hz. The price is that four levels sit closer together, so the same noise causes more errors; the error probability of 5.6 depends on that spacing.

items: The criterion does not demand a sinc; any p(t) with those zeros works.
It removes ISI only. Noise, crosstalk and interference remain.
It fixes where to sample, not when the clock actually arrives; timing error shifts the zeros away from the sampling instants.

figure.caption: Two sinc pulses one symbol period apart, and their sum. At every sampling instant the other pulse is exactly zero, so the sum reads exactly the height of the pulse that owns that instant.

spec.aria: Two sinc pulses one symbol period apart, and their sum, which passes through 1 at each sampling instant because the other pulse is exactly zero there.

examples.question: A binary baseband link sends 2400 bit/s using Nyquist-shaped pulses. The overall pulse has p(0) = 1 and p(±T) = 0.25, with all other samples zero. Around the k-th symbol the levels are a<sub>k−1</sub> = +1, a<sub>k</sub> = −1, a<sub>k+1</sub> = +1. Find the symbol rate and symbol period, the minimum Nyquist bandwidth, the ISI at the k-th sampling instant, and the sampled value. Compare the sample with the decision threshold.
steps: Binary means M = 2, so log₂M = 1 and R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/log₂M = 2400/1 = 2400 baud.
Symbol period T = 1/R<sub>s</sub> = 1/2400 s = 4.1667 × 10⁻⁴ s = 416.7 µs.
Minimum Nyquist bandwidth W = R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 2400/2 = 1200 Hz.
The wanted amplitude is 1 and the decision threshold for ±1 levels sits at 0. The sample of −0.5 is only half of 1 away from the wanted −1, so ISI has eaten half the margin.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 2400 baud, T = 416.7 µs, W = 1200 Hz, ISI = +0.5 and the sample is −0.5, half the wanted amplitude of 1.
examples.check:
Rs = 2400.0
T = 1.0/Rs
print(Rs)
print(round(T*1e6, 1))
print(Rs/2)
y = (-1)*1.0 + 1.0*0.25 + 1.0*0.25
print(y)

traps: Using R<sub>s</sub> where R<sub>s</sub>/2 belongs. The minimum baseband bandwidth is half the symbol rate, so 2400 baud needs 1200 Hz.
Mixing bit rate with symbol rate. R<sub>b</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> log₂M, so 2 bit/s/Hz holds for binary only; M-level PAM reaches 2 log₂M bit/s/Hz.
Blaming the transmit filter for ISI. The zeros are set by the overall response g<sub>T</sub> * c * g<sub>R</sub>, and a bad channel alone can create ISI.
Sign slips in the ISI sum. ISI adds algebraically with the sign of each neighbour, so a positive neighbour on a −1 symbol pulls the sample up towards the threshold.
Assuming the sinc can be built. It is non-causal and infinite; truncating it or mis-timing the sampler brings the ISI back.

quiz.q: State Nyquist's first criterion for zero ISI.
quiz.a: p(nT) = 0 for every integer n ≠ 0, where p(t) is the overall pulse from transmit filter through channel to receive filter, and T is the symbol period.

quiz.q: Why does the sinc pulse satisfy the zero-ISI condition?
quiz.a: p(t) = sin(πt/T)/(πt/T) has numerator zero whenever t/T is a nonzero integer, so the pulse for symbol k is exactly zero at every other sampling instant nT, n ≠ k.

quiz.q: A 4-level PAM system runs at 4800 baud with Nyquist pulses. Find the minimum bandwidth, the bit rate and the bandwidth efficiency.
quiz.a: W = R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 4800/2 = 2400 Hz. R<sub>b</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> log₂4 = 4800 × 2 = 9600 bit/s. Efficiency = 9600/2400 = 4 bit/s/Hz, which equals 2 log₂4.

quiz.q: The overall pulse has p(0) = 2 and p(±T) = 0.3, all other samples zero. The symbols are a<sub>k−1</sub> = +1, a<sub>k</sub> = +1, a<sub>k+1</sub> = +1. Find the ISI, the received sample and the peak distortion.
quiz.a: ISI = 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6. Sample = (1)(2) + 0.6 = 2.6. Peak distortion = 0.6/2 = 0.3, that is 30% of the wanted amplitude.

quiz.q: An ideal rectangular NRZ pulse of width T is zero at every other sampling instant, so it meets the zero-ISI condition on paper. Explain why it still fails in a real link.
quiz.a: p(nT) = 0 for n ≠ 0, so there is no ISI at the ideal sampling instants. But its spectrum is T·sinc(fT): the sinc has unbounded width and its envelope decays only as 1/f, so it does not vanish outside any finite band. Undistorted transmission needs infinite bandwidth. Any real channel or filter of finite bandwidth rounds the edges, the pulse spreads past its T-second slot, and the tails land on the neighbouring samples as ISI.

quiz.q: The sampling clock drifts by 5% of a symbol period. Using the sinc pulse, explain what happens to the ISI.
quiz.a: Sampling at kT + 0.05T gives y = a<sub>k</sub> p(0.05T) + Σ<sub>n≠k</sub> a<sub>n</sub> p((k−n)T + 0.05T). The wanted sample drops slightly to p(0.05T). Each neighbour's tail no longer sits at its zero, so the ISI sum is nonzero even though it was exactly zero at the ideal instants. For an ideal sinc the timing-error ISI sum diverges; truncating the pulse keeps it finite but still large.

quiz.q: Define peak distortion and say what value means no ISI.
quiz.a: D = (1/p(0)) Σ<sub>n≠k</sub> |p(nT)|, the worst-case ISI as a fraction of the wanted amplitude p(0). D = 0 means zero ISI.

quiz.q: Why is the sinc pulse not used in practical transmitters?
quiz.a: It is non-causal, extending from −∞ to +∞, so it cannot be generated with finite delay, and its 1/t tails decay slowly, so truncation or timing error leaves significant residual ISI.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern links push past the Nyquist rate deliberately: faster-than-Nyquist signalling packs symbols closer than T and then removes the known ISI with a detector instead of a filter. Partial response and correlative coding take the other route, adding a controlled, known ISI that is undone at the receiver, which is how some DSL and digital microwave links work. Search for Nyquist pulse shaping, faster-than-Nyquist signalling and partial response signalling to go further.
